Title: Congress voted to censure each other as many times in the last week as it did in the last two years

Summary: 
The U.S. House of Representatives voted on three censure resolutions in one week—matching the total number of censure votes in the entire 118th Congress (2023–2025). These included a rebuke of retiring Illinois Democrat Jesus 'Chuy' Garcia by Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez over allegations of election subversion, a failed motion to reprimand U.S. Virgin Islands Del. Stacey Plaskett by Rep. Ralph Norman due to her past contact with Jeffrey Epstein, and a failed attempt by Rep. Nancy Mace to censure Florida Rep. Cory Mills over alleged corruption, which was referred to the House Ethics Committee. No censure votes occurred in either chamber during the 2022 or 2024 calendar years, making the recent surge unprecedented. Censure resolutions, authorized under Article I, Section 5 of the U.S. Constitution, allow Congress to formally reprimand members, officials, or judges and can result in penalties like loss of committee assignments. While censures of non-members lack binding disciplinary power, they carry significant symbolic weight. The spike in censure attempts has prompted bipartisan concern, with Virginia Democrat Don Beyer and Nebraska Republican Don Bacon proposing legislation to raise the threshold for censure from a simple majority to 60%. They argue the process has become a tool for political grandstanding, undermining civil discourse and bypassing the Ethics Committee. Minnesota Democrat Ilhan Omar criticized the trend, saying censure is being exploited for fundraising and media attention. Former Republican congresswoman Barbara Comstock attributed the shift to a decline in political shame, noting that in the past, members would resign after serious allegations rather than endure public rebuke, a norm she blames on the influence of former President Donald Trump.

Title: Effort to expel Florida congresswoman joins rush of reprimands

Summary: 
An effort to expel Florida Congresswoman Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick from Congress has emerged amid a surge of formal reprimands among House lawmakers. On November 19, Cherfilus-McCormick was indicted on charges of stealing $5 million in federal disaster aid and using some of it for her election campaign. In response, Rep. Greg Steube, R-Florida, announced he would pursue censure and later filed legislation to initiate expulsion proceedings, which remain pending. Cherfilus-McCormick, who posted bond and denied wrongdoing, has no plans to resign and stepped down from her role as top Democrat on a Senate Foreign Affairs subcommittee per Democratic caucus rules. This incident is part of a broader trend: six other reprimand measures were filed last week, citing misconduct ranging from election subversion and false military award claims to profiting from government contracts and past communications with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Formal rebukes are rare in the House; typically, allegations are referred to the House Ethics Committee, which has not yet released a report on Cherfilus-McCormick’s case. Steube has stated he will not push for an expulsion vote until the committee acts. Expulsion requires a two-thirds majority—only six members have been expelled in U.S. history, with the most recent being Rep. George Santos, R-New York, expelled in 2023 after the Ethics Committee found he misused campaign funds, committed fraud, and filed false reports. Santos served three months of a seven-year sentence before President Donald Trump commuted it in October. Cherfilus-McCormick is not the only Floridian facing scrutiny: Rep. The House voted on November 19 to refer Mace’s censure attempt to the Ethics Committee, which established a subcommittee to investigate.

Title: Los legisladores exigen cambios en las normas de censura de la Cámara tras el "sinsentido del patio de recreo" que envuelve al Congreso

Summary: 
Legislators on both sides of the aisle in the U.S. House of Representatives are expressing growing frustration over the increased use of censure procedures, describing them as 'a playground nonsense' and a distraction from substantive legislative work. Since the end of a 43-day government shutdown on October 1, 2024, the House has seen five censure threats in just five days, including three 'privileged resolutions' forcing immediate votes on reprimanding colleagues. Representative Mike Lawler (R-NY) called the wave of censures 'the greatest collection of nonsense,' urging reforms to prevent individual members from using the process for personal attention or political gain. Some lawmakers worry the tool could be weaponized for electoral strategy. Currently, any member can initiate a censure motion, and both parties have used it multiple times this week. A bipartisan proposal seeks to raise the threshold for censure from a simple majority to 60% of the House. However, experts like Jim Curry of the University of Utah question whether this change would deter the behavior, noting the media attention and headline value that drives individual members to initiate such actions. Representative Wesley Bell (D-MO) criticized the use of censure as 'eye for an eye,' arguing it should not be used for personal grievances. Others, including Republican Mike Haridopolos (FL) and Nick LaLota (R-NY), attributed the surge to pent-up political frustration and media-driven clickbait. The House Ethics Committee, led by Republican Michael Guest (MS), is seen by some as a more appropriate venue for handling misconduct, with Representative Glenn Ivey (D-MD) noting the House has other tools like stripping committee assignments. Several members, including Jim McGovern (D-MA) and Brad Knott (R-NC), expressed concern that censure votes divert time from pressing issues like affordability and healthcare. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) acknowledged the debate and said he is open to reforms, stating he is reviewing input from members across the conference.

The Senate then passed a continuing appropriations resolution to reopen the government until January 30, but Democrats were outraged over the failure to restore Affordable Care Act subsidies. The House responded with three censure attempts: one succeeded against Rep. Chuy Garcia (D-Ill.) for withdrawing from re-election to allow his chief of staff to run; one failed against Del. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) introduced the censure motion, which was referred to the Ethics Committee by Mills’s motion, passing 310 to 103. A fourth resolution, introduced by Rep. Greg Steube (R-Fla.), seeks to expel Rep. Don Beyer (D-VA) and Don Bacon (R-NE) echoed this sentiment, stating the censure process is 'broken' and undermines the House’s ability to address national issues. Historically, censure has been rare—only 23 cases between 1832 and 2021, with no censures from 1983 to 2010. Since 2021, however, five members have been formally censured: Rep. Paul Gosar (R-AZ) and four Democrats—Rashida Tlaib (D-MI), Al Green (D-TX), Adam Schiff (D-CA), and Jamaal Bowman (D-NY). Recent censure attempts, including those led by Rep. Nancy Mace (R-SC) against Cory Mills (R-FL), Chuy García (D-IL), and Ilhan Omar (D-MN), have been widely seen as partisan. Chu voted against censuring Mills, Plaskett (D-VI), and Omar, noting that such actions often serve as political theater or fundraising tools. She highlighted a 'revenge motive' driving the cycle, where one party’s censure prompts retaliation from the other. The House retains broad power to discipline members, with expulsion as the most severe penalty, followed by censure and reprimand. Censure requires a majority vote and involves a public reading of the resolution in the chamber, symbolizing deep disapproval without meeting expulsion standards.

articles.title: House resolution seeks to raise threshhold for censuring member to 60% - UPI.com
articles.summary: A bipartisan resolution co-sponsored by U.S. Representatives Don Beyer (D-Va.) and Don Bacon (R-Nebraska) proposes raising the threshold for censuring a House member from a simple majority to 60% to ensure bipartisan consensus. The measure, introduced on November 22, 2025, comes amid a surge of censure efforts targeting three members: Republican Jesus 'Chuy' Garcia of Illinois, Republican Cory Mills of Florida, and Democratic delegate Stacey Plaskett of the U.S. Virgin Islands. Beyer stated that the censure process has deteriorated from a rare, due-process-driven mechanism into a political tool, undermining the House’s functionality. Bacon echoed this, calling for 'commonsense safeguards' to counter 'mob mentality' in Congress. The resolution already had 29 sponsors by Friday afternoon. According to NBC News, the House has censured members only six times in the 21st century, with most historical censures following lengthy ethics investigations involving criminal activity or serious misconduct. Expulsion from Congress requires a two-thirds vote, with 16 members expelled during the Civil War and the most recent being George Santos, R-N.Y., who was convicted and served three months in prison before a presidential commutation. Beyer warned that the proliferation of censure attempts is unsustainable and damaging to institutional integrity. This week, the House censured Garcia for unilaterally selecting his successor after the primary filing deadline and rejected a censure of Plaskett despite her receipt of messages from convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein during a hearing. Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., introduced a censure resolution against Mills, which was referred to the Ethics Committee. Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla., threatened to censure Democratic Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick, who was indicted for allegedly stealing $5 million in federal disaster funds. The article also notes that President Donald Trump met with New York City mayor-elect Zohran Mamdani in the Oval Office on Friday, November 22, 2025.

Stacey Plaskett (D-U.S. Virgin Islands) over past communications with Jeffrey Epstein. Rep. Greg Steube (R-Fla.) announced plans to push a censure vote against Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick (D-Fla.), who was indicted that day for allegedly stealing $5 million in FEMA overpayments. Four censure resolutions were introduced in two days, reflecting a growing trend of partisan finger-pointing and virtue signaling. Notably, the Garcia reprimand was introduced by Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, and the Mills censure was sponsored by Republican Nancy Mace, indicating cross-party retaliation. They described the reform as a 'sensible' fix to a broken process. Connecticut Democrat Jim Himes endorsed the move, calling the current cycle 'bullshit' and urging 'shut this shit down' due to the lack of due process. A 60% threshold would likely prevent purely partisan censure attempts and restore rhetorical condemnation over formal measures, avoiding a potential 'mutually assured destruction' scenario in the House.

articles.title: WATCH LIVE: House gets back to business with agenda focused on censures and investigations
articles.summary: The U.S. House of Representatives reconvened after a multi-week hiatus, but its agenda has been dominated by a surge in censure and reprimand efforts against members, leaving little time for legislative work. House Speaker Mike Johnson, facing a narrow Republican majority, has struggled to maintain control as rank-and-file lawmakers increasingly use tools like discharge petitions to bypass leadership. Notable actions include a failed effort to censure Del. Stacey Plaskett, R-Fla., over text messages from Jeffrey Epstein during a 2019 hearing, which passed 214-209; a vote to reprimand Rep. Jesus 'Chuy' Garcia, D-Ill., after his chief of staff filed paperwork to run for his seat; and a filing to censure Rep. Cory Mills, R-Fla., following a judge’s protective order against him over allegations of threats and non-consensual image sharing. Additionally, Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla., plans to file a motion to censure Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick, D-Fla., who faces federal charges of stealing $5 million in disaster funds. The House also voted 236-186 to reprimand Garcia. Despite Speaker Johnson’s push for a 'normal' legislative process, lawmakers across parties view this level of disruption as the new norm. Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries criticized Republicans for failing to advance bills on pressing issues like the expiration of health care tax credits on December 31, which could leave millions without affordable insurance. The House has shown little progress on routine government funding or addressing the high cost of living. The release of the Jeffrey Epstein files, initially blocked by leadership, was forced through after a nearly unanimous discharge petition, highlighting the growing power of rank-and-file members to override speaker authority.
